title: LPT Comprehensive Review — Exam Form 1 (Mixed Blueprint)
subtitle: Phase-3 cumulative review: 20 blueprint-weighted single-best-answer items spanning all four LPT domains (Mental Health Care ~45%, Basic Nursing Care ~22%, Developmental Disabilities ~18%, Legal & Ethical ~15%). Exam-style mixed practice drawing on high-yield concepts from across the foundation and depth sets.
scenario: A short, mixed, blueprint-weighted review form: the questions jump across all four LPT content areas the way the real exam does, so you practice recognizing what kind of problem you're facing and choosing the best action under time.

steps.q: A client says, 'I don't really see the point in anything anymore.' The MOST therapeutic response is:

opts.text: 'You shouldn't feel that way—things will get better.'
opts.rat: This is false reassurance; it dismisses the client's feelings and shuts down exploration.

opts.text: 'Can you tell me more about what you're feeling right now?'
opts.rat: An open-ended, exploring response invites the client to share and signals the technician is listening—and it opens the door to assessing safety.

opts.text: 'Everyone feels down sometimes; it will pass.'
opts.rat: This minimizes the client's experience and is nontherapeutic.

opts.text: 'Let's talk about something more positive.'
opts.rat: Changing the subject avoids the client's distress and blocks communication.

steps.q: A client expresses deep hopelessness. Regarding suicide risk, the technician should:

opts.text: Avoid mentioning suicide so as not to put the idea in the client's head
opts.rat: Asking directly about suicide does not plant the idea; avoiding it can miss a life-threatening risk.

opts.text: Change the subject to something cheerful
opts.rat: Avoiding the topic fails to assess a potentially urgent safety risk.

opts.text: Directly ask whether the client is thinking about suicide and assess for a plan
opts.rat: Direct questioning is appropriate and does not increase risk; it allows assessment of a plan and means so the client can be kept safe.

opts.text: Simply reassure the client that they have much to live for
opts.rat: False reassurance does not assess risk and can feel dismissive.

steps.q: A client on an antipsychotic develops a high fever, severe 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, and confusion with unstable vital signs. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Hold the antipsychotic and report immediately as a possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome emergency
opts.rat: Fever, rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability suggest NMS—a medical emergency requiring the drug to be held and urgent reporting.

opts.text: Give the next dose of the antipsychotic to calm the client
opts.rat: More antipsychotic worsens NMS; the drug is held.

opts.text: Encourage fluids and reassess on the next shift
opts.rat: NMS is an emergency requiring immediate action, not delayed reassessment.

opts.text: Assume it is an expected effect of the medication
opts.rat: These findings are an emergency, not an expected effect.

steps.q: Which instruction is correct teaching for a client taking lithium?

opts.text: Sharply cut back on all salt and fluids
opts.rat: A sudden drop in sodium or fluids can raise lithium to a toxic level.

opts.text: Skip doses on days you feel well
opts.rat: Skipping doses destabilizes therapy; lithium is taken consistently as prescribed.

opts.text: Stop lithium on your own during hot weather
opts.rat: Stopping lithium is a prescriber decision; the client reports concerns rather than self-discontinuing.

opts.text: Keep fluid and salt intake consistent and keep lab-monitoring appointments
opts.rat: Steady fluid and sodium intake and regular blood-level monitoring keep lithium in a safe, effective range.

steps.q: A client who had an angry outburst insists, 'He started it—he's the one who's always hostile,' when in fact the client was the aggressor. This defense mechanism is:

opts.text: Projection
opts.rat: Projection is attributing one's own unacceptable feelings or behavior to someone else—here, the client's own hostility is assigned to the peer.

opts.text: Sublimation
opts.rat: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into acceptable activities, not blaming others.

opts.text: Regression
opts.rat: Regression is returning to earlier, less mature behavior.

opts.text: Compensation
opts.rat: Compensation is offsetting a perceived weakness by excelling in another area.

steps.q: A client is having a panic attack with rapid breathing and intense fear. The BEST intervention is to:

opts.text: Leave the client alone to calm down
opts.rat: Leaving a panicking client alone can heighten fear; staying provides safety and support.

opts.text: Stay with the client, remain calm, and guide slow breathing in a low-stimulation setting
opts.rat: A calm presence, simple guidance for slow breathing, and reduced stimulation help the client regain control during a panic attack.

opts.text: Explain the detailed physiology of anxiety
opts.rat: A panicking client cannot process a detailed explanation; simple, calm guidance is used.

opts.text: Tell the client to 'snap out of it'
opts.rat: This is dismissive and nontherapeutic and can worsen distress.

steps.q: When verbally de-escalating a client who is becoming agitated, the technician should:

opts.text: Stand close and match the client's raised voice to show authority
opts.rat: Crowding and raising one's voice escalate the client.

opts.text: Issue rapid ultimatums and threats
opts.rat: Ultimatums and threats increase agitation.

opts.text: Use a calm voice, maintain a non-threatening stance, and give the client space
opts.rat: A calm tone, non-threatening posture, and adequate personal space support de-escalation and safety.

opts.text: Touch the client to reassure them
opts.rat: Unexpected touch can be perceived as threatening and may escalate an agitated client.

steps.q: A client abruptly stops long-term heavy alcohol use. Compared with opioid withdrawal, alcohol withdrawal is:

opts.text: Potentially life-threatening, with a risk of seizures and delirium tremens
opts.rat: Alcohol withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens and is potentially life-threatening, unlike opioid withdrawal, which is very uncomfortable but usually not directly lethal.

opts.text: Always milder and never dangerous
opts.rat: Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous, not always mild.

opts.text: Only a psychological craving with no physical risk
opts.rat: Alcohol withdrawal has serious physical risks, including seizures.

opts.text: Identical in danger to caffeine withdrawal
opts.rat: Caffeine withdrawal is not life-threatening; alcohol withdrawal can be.

steps.q: A client experiencing frightening auditory hallucinations looks scared. The BEST response is to:

opts.text: Argue that the voices are not real and the client is mistaken
opts.rat: Arguing is nontherapeutic and can increase distress; reality is presented calmly, not by debating.

opts.text: Pretend to hear the voices too
opts.rat: Reinforcing the hallucination is not appropriate.

opts.text: Ignore the client entirely
opts.rat: Ignoring the frightened client abandons them; support and calm reality are provided.

opts.text: Acknowledge the client's fear without reinforcing the hallucination, and calmly present reality
opts.rat: Validating the client's fear while calmly offering reality supports safety and trust without confirming the hallucination.

steps.q: The single most effective way for the technician to prevent the spread of infection is:

opts.text: Keeping the unit dimly lit
opts.rat: Lighting does not control infection spread.

opts.text: Limiting clients' fluid intake
opts.rat: Restricting fluids does not prevent infection and can harm clients.

opts.text: Wearing a gown for every interaction
opts.rat: A gown is used for specific precautions but is not the single most effective general measure.

opts.text: Performing proper hand hygiene
opts.rat: Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infection.

steps.q: A conscious client with diabetes who can swallow safely shows signs of a low blood glucose. Applying the 'rule of 15,' the technician should:

opts.text: Give a dose of insulin
opts.rat: Insulin lowers glucose further and would worsen a low.

opts.text: Give about 15 grams of a fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck in about 15 minutes
opts.rat: The rule of 15 is ~15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait ~15 minutes, and recheck, repeating if the low persists.

opts.text: Withhold all food and fluids
opts.rat: Withholding food leaves the low untreated.

opts.text: Have the client exercise to raise the glucose
opts.rat: Exercise can lower glucose further and is unsafe during a low.

steps.q: An EARLY sign of inadequate oxygenation (hypoxia) that the technician should recognize is:

opts.text: Deep, restful sleep
opts.rat: Restful sleep is not a sign of hypoxia.

opts.text: Slow, relaxed breathing
opts.rat: Hypoxia more often causes increased respiratory effort, not slow relaxed breathing.

opts.text: Restlessness and anxiety
opts.rat: Restlessness and anxiety are early signs of hypoxia, often appearing before cyanosis (a late sign).

opts.text: Warm, pink skin
opts.rat: Warm, pink skin is a normal finding, not an early sign of hypoxia.

steps.q: While eating, a client suddenly cannot speak, cough, or breathe and clutches the throat. The technician should:

opts.text: Offer a glass of water to wash it down
opts.rat: Giving fluids to a choking client is unsafe.

opts.text: Wait quietly to see if it clears on its own
opts.rat: Complete airway obstruction requires immediate intervention, not waiting.

opts.text: Have the client lie flat and rest
opts.rat: Lying flat does not relieve the obstruction and delays intervention.

opts.text: Recognize complete airway obstruction, begin abdominal thrusts, and call for help
opts.rat: Inability to speak, cough, or breathe signals complete obstruction; abdominal thrusts are started at once while help is summoned.

steps.q: A nonverbal client with a developmental disability suddenly begins hitting the side of their own head. The technician should FIRST:

opts.text: Ensure safety and look for an unmet need or a source of pain the behavior may be communicating
opts.rat: Behavior is communication; ensuring safety and investigating an unmet need or pain addresses the cause of new self-injury.

opts.text: Assume the behavior is meaningless and ignore it
opts.rat: New self-injury may signal pain or an unmet need and is not ignored.

opts.text: Punish the client for the behavior
opts.rat: Punishment is nontherapeutic and does not address the cause.

opts.text: Immediately place the client in restraints
opts.rat: Restraint is not the first response; safety and identifying the cause come first.

steps.q: During a client's generalized seizure, the technician should:

opts.text: Hold the client still to stop the movements
opts.rat: Restraining a seizing client can cause injury and does not stop the seizure.

opts.text: Protect the client from injury, avoid restraining them, and put nothing in the mouth
opts.rat: Seizure safety means protecting from injury, not restraining, and never placing anything in the mouth.

opts.text: Place a padded object in the client's mouth
opts.rat: Nothing is placed in the mouth; it can cause injury or airway obstruction.

opts.text: Leave the client unattended during the seizure
opts.rat: The client is not left alone; they are protected and monitored.

steps.q: To reduce aspiration risk at mealtime for a client with dysphagia, the technician should:

opts.text: Feed the client quickly while they are reclined
opts.rat: Feeding a reclined client quickly greatly increases aspiration risk.

opts.text: Encourage large, rapid bites to finish sooner
opts.rat: Large, rapid bites raise choking and aspiration risk.

opts.text: Position the client upright, use recommended food textures, and provide unhurried supervision
opts.rat: Upright positioning, appropriate textures, and calm supervision reduce aspiration risk in dysphagia.

opts.text: Leave the client to eat alone
opts.rat: A client at aspiration risk needs supervision, not to be left alone.

steps.q: Services and interventions for a client with a developmental disability should be:

opts.text: As restrictive as possible for staff convenience
opts.rat: Care uses the least restrictive approach, not the most restrictive for convenience.

opts.text: Decided without input from the client or their team
opts.rat: The client and their team are included in planning; person-centered care is required.

opts.text: Focused only on what the client cannot do
opts.rat: Person-centered care builds on the client's strengths, not only deficits.

opts.text: Provided in the least restrictive manner that meets the client's needs, respecting their rights
opts.rat: The least-restrictive, rights-respecting, person-centered approach guides care for clients with developmental disabilities.

steps.q: Under California law, a person may be placed on a 72-hour involuntary hold (a '5150') when, as a result of a mental health disorder, they are:

opts.text: A danger to self, a danger to others, or gravely disabled
opts.rat: The 5150 criteria are danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability due to a mental health disorder.

opts.text: Merely uncooperative with staff
opts.rat: Being uncooperative does not meet the legal criteria for an involuntary hold.

opts.text: Refusing to attend a group activity
opts.rat: Refusing an activity is not grounds for a hold.

opts.text: Asking to leave when there is no safety concern
opts.rat: Wanting to leave, without meeting the danger/grave-disability criteria, is not grounds for a hold.

steps.q: A technician has a reasonable suspicion that a dependent-adult client is being abused. As a mandated reporter, the technician should:

opts.text: Investigate and gather proof before reporting
opts.rat: Mandated reporters do not need to prove abuse; reasonable suspicion is the trigger to report.

opts.text: Report the reasonable suspicion as required, without having to prove it first
opts.rat: A mandated reporter reports on reasonable suspicion; proof is not required and gathering it is not the reporter's role.

opts.text: Keep it confidential to protect the client
opts.rat: Mandated reporting is a legal duty that overrides ordinary confidentiality for suspected abuse.

opts.text: Wait until they are completely certain before telling anyone
opts.rat: Waiting for certainty delays required reporting; reasonable suspicion is enough.

steps.q: A client's family member phones and asks for details about the client's condition. The technician should:

opts.text: Share all details, since the caller is family
opts.rat: Being family does not authorize disclosure of protected health information.

opts.text: Confirm only the client's diagnosis
opts.rat: Even the diagnosis is protected and is not disclosed without authorization.

opts.text: Not disclose protected information without proper authorization, following confidentiality rules
opts.rat: Protected health information is not released without proper authorization; confidentiality is maintained.

opts.text: Post an update in an area where any staff can see it
opts.rat: Posting client information openly violates confidentiality.

reference: LPT Comprehensive Review — Exam Form 1 (Phase-3). A blueprint-weighted, cumulative mixed-review form for the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician program, sampling high-yield concepts across all four content areas in approximately the exam's proportions (Mental Health Care ~45%: therapeutic communication, direct suicide assessment, NMS recognition, lithium teaching, defense mechanisms, panic-attack intervention, verbal de-escalation, alcohol-withdrawal danger, and responding to hallucinations; Basic Nursing Care ~22%: hand hygiene as the top infection-control measure, the rule of 15 for hypoglycemia, restlessness/anxiety as an early hypoxia sign, and complete-airway-obstruction/choking response; Developmental Disabilities ~18%: behavior-as-communication and self-injury, seizure safety, dysphagia/aspiration positioning, and least-restrictive rights-respecting care; Legal & Ethical ~15%: 5150 involuntary-hold criteria, mandated reporting on reasonable suspicion, and confidentiality of protected information). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references; concepts are stated conceptually and no specific drug doses, lab values, or numeric cutoffs are asserted (the rule of 15 uses the standard ~15 g / ~15 min teaching). Content draws on and does not introduce new material beyond the foundation (mh-core, bnc-core, dd-core, legal-core) and Phase-2 depth (mh-core-21..32) sets. Reviewed by Joseph Ongongo, LPT.
